reviews.text: Really like the game, but the Snow-Melter boss during the final act is literally impossible to defeat (unless your build is broken enough to somehow do it within two turns). After three turns, he activates all three torches making himself invincible, and as far as I can tell there is no way to extinguish the torches and the battle just keeps going forever until you either lose or give up. Will change to a positive review if and when this is somehow fixed. EDIT: I played through the game a couple more times and the boss' mechanic DOES work as intended. That being, when you summon units in a specific lane it will either light or extinguish the candle within the corresponding lane. However, when using the Light-catcher archive in combination with the Amalgest it becomes virtually impossible to defeat the snow melter. This is because the combination of these two relics causes all summons to occur twice (as all cards become exhausts and all exhausts are played twice). Therefore, the Snow-melters candles are triggered twice every time the player summons units, causing the candles to go off and then back on again (or vice versa) making it effectively impossible to defeat that boss with this specific build, as you physically cannot extinguish any candles once they have been lit. I've decided to change my review to positive given that it's a minor problem but I still think it should be worked on. TLDR: I got ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because my build was too good.

给好评纯是因为demo玩了30小时，而且还能继续玩，但正式版只能呵呵。 内测转正式难受点：1.试玩版几十小时积累的资源不能继承我忍，但新手教程不能跳过什么意思？2.英雄、卡牌以及遗物基本都有等级和解锁限制，想玩喜欢的、拿手的流派，如骑兵流得先打1小时解锁，玩萨拉丁自由部署、玩矮人啤酒更是得先难受几个小时。3.给流派关键牌的机率一如既往的恶心人，想要卡牌和遗物重选至少得打到第三章8次花上五六个小时。（一次500，一次40分钟。我是说游戏）4.正式版卡牌的改动和增量是真的难评。有些还没解锁不好说，但弱势的爆炸着火流还是没动。实测里两张“原住民移民+”互相叠加等于无限次数召唤，只要有合适的遗物算是无敌；宿命之日可以改成打首领战五个回合后自动认输吗？神之一手之他没有把卡牌放在召唤位里，自动判负。5.正式版第三章兽人的难度有点恐怖，牌组稍差一点可能普通关都无损。对新手真的友好吗？6.可能习惯了以前的界面，字面变小有点难受。而且游戏内料理槽位置和地图感觉也更差了。 总之一句话，正式版等于把demo玩家一刀切割了。所有新老玩家一切从0开始。只是中国有句古话叫做：“由简入奢易，由奢如简难。”一个单机游戏，我“免费的demo”投入了几十小时算是淹没成本吧，但既往的经验和资源积累已经形成了舒适区，（难得有时间上号，就是冲着玩骑兵流，玩自由部署去的，但是不行。还没解锁，能玩了不能刷新卡牌也难受）花了钱还需要我去“付费的正版”里重新花上10小时积累。有种野路子高中生必须读正规义务教育九年才能高考的感觉。公平但那真的合理吗？ 最后游戏是真的好玩，祝大卖。只是应该有很多老玩家都不想再花费低质时间，去玩一款熟悉的新游戏吧。玩游戏是为了开心，希望能说一句：demo继承！算是那句古话，识时务者为俊杰吧，求求了。

优点好评都说了那我就不说了，我说一说缺点吧。我原本以为拿到念珠和消耗发动两次这两件遗物我就无敌了，直到我遇到隐藏boss，制作组恶意太大了，这是人能想出来的怪？ 很难想象都2025年了还有游戏改不了分辨率，4k下糊也就算了字还小。 首通之后退出来写测评眼睛都是花的 TAT 1.制作组没必要再帮卡牌效果想一个其它名字，不如就叫战吼、亡语之类的，方便理解让新手更快上手 2.章节之间难度跨度太大，基本第一章都能无伤刷，然后第二章就被精英怪无伤刷，第三章更是不用说（那个b兽人猛的不像话，而且这还是小怪） 3.boss奖励及其不合理，打完boss血不会自动回满，还得遗物血量二选一，拿遗物还要扣血量上限（虽然加血上限的牌有很多，但是很多情况下都是要通关了才能拿到，非酋都哭晕了） 4.部分卡牌文本真应该优化了，不是字越多越容易理解。而且我搞不懂一点的是为什么有些卡有词条解释但是有些就没有？我还得先拿了打出来我才知道效果。 5.分辨率问题，这里不再赘述 6.ui得优化一下（这里点名批评回合结束可以保留一张牌，每次选好牌要点确定，都会莫名其妙点到其他手牌） 7.局外成长，个人觉得有点肝了，但这里也可以理解，不过我还是希望减轻点肝度。

Commander Quest [code] [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36948155-Card-Game-KING/] FOR MORE CARD AND BOARD GAMES FOLLOW US [b]CARD GAME KING [/b][/url] [/code] Despite the uninspired name, Commander Quest is a competently made deckbuilder/army summoner hybrid and I don't think it fully deserves all the flak it's getting. To briefly describe the game: it's a roguelike where you build a deck and use it to summon units on different paths or cast spells. The goal of each battle is to kill the enemy leader which also summons units. I like the gameplay and there is a surprising creativity in level and enemy design that keeps the game from feeling too repetitive. That said, the game did receive a fair amount of criticism from others and I would like to address each one based on my own experience. One big complaints is about the game's difficulty. While it's true that there are spikes in difficulty from the 2nd boss onward, it feels challenging but not impossible. Some people mentioned that because of the difficulty it requires specific cards to beat, but I didn't find it to be true, although partially because devs are fairly active in balancing the game so some unfair battles have already been nerfed within days of release. The second criticism brought up is the lack of variety in builds. In my playthroughs several very different strategies proved to be viable and don't see it currently as a big issue, but I will say that sometimes, you really don't get the right cards to make a combo work. The final negative that is being brought up is the low amount of content and variety. I do agree that the overall card pool for each race is fairly small, but the game has several classes that play quite differently and there is even variety within a class due to different starting relics. On top of that each class can play as human or dwarf race which has their own deck of units that are available. It would've been great if there was one more race or at least more cards per race, but the current level of variety felt fine to me. Between classes, cards and relics there are always some new things that can be done differently between runs. My only gripe with the game is the run length which can easily exceed 2h, and it feels bad to need to start over because one battle went poorly. Overall, I enjoyed Commander Quest and the ongoing effort of devs to make the game even better, makes me like it even more. [h1][b]The positive[/b] [/h1] + Fun army summoner and deckbuilder hybrid + Good variety between classes, cards and relics. + Creative enemy and map design + Very polished UI and gameplay [h1][b]The neutral[/b][/h1] * Not a fan of the last boss design as it plays differently than the rest of the game [h1][b]The negative[/b][/h1] - Some remaining balance issues. - Runs take too long. 2-3 hours per run feels too much. - Card pool per race is fairly small [h1][b]Conclusion:[/b] [/h1] Building decks and summoning armies against creative enemy design is a lot of fun. Fairly challenging but runs are a bit too long. Recommended.

It DOES feel like progress is quite slow in terms of unlocks which would be fine if the game was just a little more fun. As it is, it's not grabbed me quite as much as I would have liked. Many of the battles also feel like a slog of both sides sending endless units at each other that never actually get as far as the enemy commander! There doesn't appear to be much in the way of combos with units and spells, so it's more a case of just getting on with it and testing your own patience at times.

TLDR: I don't find RNG-based "difficulty" to be fun. I really want to recommend this game. I love the entire idea behind it. However, I just re-downloaded it after taking a break for quite a while, and nothing seems to have changed. My gripe is that while it's super challenging, it feels artificial. The game itself wouldn't be so bad if there were any way to get the cards or relics you need, but there isn't even rerolling for anything (unless I'm forgetting a rare relic that allows it). The vast majority of what you're offered won't work with the strategy you decide to go for. At least, that's why I assume the commanders get special perks for specific playstyles. You can usually get through to the first boss just by being good at countering where the AI places units, but then comes the first boss, with abilities that will tear through what you get in your default deck. It's not too bad when all you have to do is delay him, but if you actually have to kill him on a timer, then you'd better hope RNG rolled in your favor and gave you one to three strong cards, events, or relics that can turn a run from a failure into a success. And even in the runs where I do get a great combo, there are so few chances to trim or buff my deck that the original cards mostly sit there, taking up space like a millstone.

Not as much control as I would want in a game strategy game. It's more progression based than skill based. It's a rogue-lite so it going to be seemingly unfair/randomly scaled until you've invested probably 10 plus hours into it. Even then, it's still 90% luck. Imagine playing chess but you have to draw your pieces like yugioh cards. You can't count cards because your discard pile and your deck are essentially one in the same. Basically, you can get lucky and draw rooks and multiple queens in a few hands, but 80+ percent of the time you're drawing straight pawns. Everything is so RNG based that you're actually not strategizing when you think about it. You just play the logical cards that any half-brain would pick when the game is gracious enough to give it you. So when you really think about it, you're actually just playing the card game "war" (that game where you just split a deck in half with someone else and you both flip one card off the top of the deck - highest card wins). Ol' heart of the cards playing ahh game. The only actually not-as-much-luck based strategy in this game is to thin your deck to increase the frequency to draw the cards you want. Even then, you're only guaranteed 3 opportunities to remove 1 card at a time from the 10 cards you start with - and you have to spend resources (that you hopefully have at that point) to use those opportunities. Also, I have regularly experienced bugs on this game. Half of them were during the final boss where the game would freeze. It's not just the gameplay. It seems that some of the achievements are bugged too, as I have had to complete a couple of them more then once before they finally unlocked.

Decent turnbased autobattler/TD/strategy game with Slay the Spire aspects, but with less polish and seemingly abandoned before some features were fully fleshed out. I'd say that there were a lot of parts that weren't properly playtested or properly implemented. My review is positive because the game is cheap and I got enough enjoyment early enough in my playtime that the £9.99 price is worth it. TLDR; I'd say try the demo and decide for yourself whether the cheap price is worth picking it up or not. If you enjoy the demo, the base game is that but with an extra act, more characters and a decent amount of card variety. Disregarding all the negative parts that follow: I had fun playing this game. There is enough variety to make the game replayable, I'll say it again, the game is cheap and it has a FREE version in the form of the demo that gives you two acts of FREE content. Base your decision to buy on that. Anyway, my thoughts on the game: As of now, I am one of the few people to 100% this game and this is for good reason: winning 100 runs and reaching level 20 Penance takes a torturously long time. While most runs end up feeling the same if you're trying to grind up to Penance 20 by abusing one of the many buggy mechanics this game has to get a win. Would not recommend others putting themselves through that unless they actually enjoy the added difficulty of higher Penance levels and want to be forced to learn how to min-max the game and streamline their builds. As with any game - you will get better at the game even faster if you play on harder difficulty modes, if you stay on easy you won't improve as much. The only reason I completed it 100% is because I took a few long breaks from the game and came back to it when I wasn't bored of it anymore, 100 runs weren't done in a single block of time. A lot of the comments I see on RNG taking precedence are something that I agree with - to an extent as far as early runs go since you only get rerolls after you play enough to get the ember to afford it. Which makes the initial difficulty spike of the bosses hard to overcome without good luck. Act 3 normal battles and minibosses can be harder than the bosses of previous acts, possibly even the Act 3 boss too, with some battles being gimmicks like dps checks, stealthed enemies, enemies that mimic your last summon, or adding curse cards to your deck. IMO The game only really "starts" when you unlock the option to add two of nearly any cards to the deck at the start of a run. Since this is when you're finally able to start a run with a build already half done. This is a problem because ember takes so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long to earn and the upgrades are too expensive, most people will give up before reaching this point - an arbitrary time gate on fun is not good game design. My thought is that this was done with the intention of eventually monetising it like mobile games do, but the game seems abandoned before reaching this point, probably from the lack of players caused by said choice in game design - see the irony here, classic greedy publisher choices ending up costing money instead - so the point is moot. The main reason this game is difficult is because unlike pretty much every other game, there isn't a guide on Steam to handhold you when you get stuck because of the nonexistant playerbase, it took many hours of trial and error to reach the point where I'd have to actually try to lose by picking a bad build or by trying a new mechanic. The game as it stands is "finished". Every "type" of deck can be built and won with, it just takes creativity, adapting your strategy and persistence to learn how to win in the same vein as any moderately difficult game. There is more build variety than other people are suggesting in other reviews, but there are no guides available to help you find them. Most of my enjoyment from this game came from finding all these different combinations on my own by just trying new stuff, thinking "could I build a deck centred around this mechanic?" but I also understand that most people want to have at least some guidance, especially when they find something too difficult to enjoy. The biggest issue with this game, is most people don't like to struggle bashing their heads against a deceptively difficult casual game with a massive difficulty spike, when instead they could invest their valuable time into learning something more fulfilling. For the average person, games like this one are generally played because they take less effort than something like an FPS or RTS and the effort required to learn the game well enough to win consistently goes against that grain. To play devil's advocate, losing lots of times is a staple of roguelikes in general, this isn't really any different from Slay the Spire in that regard. There are MANY bugs and unintended clashes in mechanics that cause things to function improperly. So many that I can't even remember them all. The one you'll see most often is bad pathing and summons getting stuck on the environment. One notable bug/exploit, to the player's benefit, is with the Letter of Recommendation and summons that add more units based on the other cards in your deck (Raging Tide Militia and Mercenary), due to a weird interaction, you end up with far more units with the copied card than the original, which can be abused to the point where I had the entire map filled with units in a couple of runs. As an example of where the game is going wrong, the Dwarf faction is straight up not as fun to play as the Human one. It adds a secondary resource that requires time to build up to do some extra card interactions like getting a summon with 30 health that gains 2 attack for every steel you have or the Richard relic that gives your units extra 1 health for every 20 steel. The units are all slower as well, meaning most Dwarf runs end up being: hurry up and wait. The Dwarf version of Jeanne d'Arc is flat out worse than the human version. The Ancient Rosary relic applies 1 protection to every structure unit once per turn, the Dwarf deck has no structures because the devs added a unit type and swapped the ballista to the new type without changing the relic to match, the only structure you can get at start is the culverin which I find misses way too often to be worth playing over your actual deck, especially at the cost of 2 mana. The Holy knight summon for humans gains +2/+8 for every Base card used (Slay the Spire power card), the Dwarf version stays at the fragile 8 health and gets 3 attack for every 10 steel. At the same time, one of her relics incentivises steel usage by dealing 3 damage to 3 random enemies every time you spend steel, meaning there is no synergy between that and the knights while the human version gives you a random base card every turn.
Its a tough fight to the top. Every game is different and there are many ways to win or lose. Its a Slay the Spire 2 like game, which I own too. I would rate Commander Quest higher.

Commander Quest delivers an engaging blend of roguelike deck-building and automated tactical battles, creating a strategy experience that feels both innovative and rewarding. Developed by Flyway Games, Inc. and published by Flyway Games, Inc. alongside KRAFTON, Inc., the game transports players into a whimsical fantasy world where legendary historical commanders are reimagined as heroes leading armies of mythical creatures, dwarves, beasts, and undead warriors. Rather than relying on traditional turn-based mechanics or simple card combat, the game combines careful deck construction with real-time battlefield execution, resulting in a formula that constantly challenges players to think strategically before every encounter. The foundation of the gameplay lies in assembling an effective deck while building an army capable of handling increasingly difficult battles. Every card, relic, and unit has the potential to contribute to powerful combinations, making each reward selection meaningful. Instead of chasing the strongest individual cards, success comes from understanding how different abilities interact with one another. Players can specialize in defensive formations anchored by sturdy dwarves, unleash aggressive cavalry charges, overwhelm opponents with summoned beasts, or command ghostly legions that excel through unique abilities. The wide variety of tactical possibilities encourages experimentation, ensuring that no two playthroughs feel exactly alike. Combat introduces an extra layer of depth by allowing the assembled units to automatically clash on the battlefield after deployment. Although battles resolve without direct control, preparation remains entirely in the player's hands. Positioning, deployment order, army composition, and deck synergy all determine whether a strategy succeeds or collapses under enemy pressure. This fusion of deck-building and auto-battling creates satisfying moments as carefully planned combinations unfold during combat, rewarding thoughtful decision-making instead of relying purely on chance. The game's fantasy interpretation of famous military leaders gives Commander Quest its own distinct personality. Instead of pursuing historical accuracy, it embraces creativity by placing recognizable commanders in a colorful world filled with dragons, monsters, magic, and legendary creatures. This imaginative approach allows every faction to feature memorable unit designs while maintaining a lighthearted tone that complements the game's strategic complexity. The setting feels playful without diminishing the importance of tactical planning, making the overall adventure both entertaining and approachable. Replay value is one of the game's greatest strengths. As expected from a roguelike, each run offers randomized cards, relics, encounters, and events that force players to adapt their plans as they progress. A strategy that dominates one expedition may not be possible in the next, encouraging flexibility rather than repetitive optimization. Random encounters further enrich the journey by introducing unusual merchants, mysterious experiments, magical relics, and humorous scenarios that can dramatically influence the direction of a run. These unpredictable events prevent the gameplay loop from becoming monotonous and add welcome variety between battles. Visually, Commander Quest embraces a bright fantasy art style that makes its diverse armies easy to distinguish during combat. Units feature expressive designs, battle effects remain clear without overwhelming the screen, and the interface presents the game's many mechanics in an organized manner. The battlefield remains readable even during large-scale clashes, allowing players to observe how their strategies perform while appreciating the lively animations that accompany each encounter. Combined with an atmospheric soundtrack and polished presentation, the audiovisual package complements the strategic gameplay well. The progression system rewards both patience and learning. Defeats rarely feel unfair because each failed run teaches valuable lessons about deck construction, unit placement, and synergy management. As players become more familiar with different commanders, relic combinations, and battlefield tactics, they gradually unlock stronger strategies capable of overcoming increasingly difficult challenges. While newcomers may initially find the layered mechanics intimidating, the steady sense of improvement makes mastering the game particularly satisfying. Commander Quest successfully combines several popular genres into a cohesive experience that feels fresh rather than derivative. Its emphasis on strategic planning, creative deck building, tactical army composition, and constantly changing roguelike progression gives players plenty of reasons to return for another run. Although some randomness is inherent to the genre, the game's focus on intelligent adaptation ensures that player skill remains the deciding factor far more often than luck. For fans of strategy games looking for something that blends thoughtful planning with highly replayable gameplay, Commander Quest stands as an excellent recommendation. Rating: 7/10
